title: 🌍 World Foundations & Geography
rawNotionMarkup: This page records Eryndor's physical world, large-scale geography, known regions, settlements, routes and travel assumptions. It does not attempt to provide a precise atlas where no canonical map or exact coordinates have been established. ## The world at a glance - World name: Eryndor. - Current historical period: Fifth Age, Era of Crowns. (The old label “Age of Crowns” was imprecise.) - Current year in the campaign: 3,847. - Planet type: Terrestrial, broadly Earthlike in gravity and environmental conditions. - Approximate diameter: 50,000 km in current canon (13,400 km is the superseded original draft). - Approximate surface composition: 60% water and 40% land in current canon (71% / 29% was the old draft). - Day: 24 hours. - Year: 360 days, divided into four seasons of approximately 90 days each. - Seasons: Spring, summer, autumn and winter. - Approximate planetary circumference: 157,080 km for the current 50,000-km spherical model; 42,000 km was the superseded draft. Eryndor has a wide range of climates and environments: mountain systems, forests, tundra, deserts, fertile river valleys, grasslands, high plateaus, jungles, tropical coasts, rugged shorelines, islands and deep subterranean regions. Environmental and cultural diversity is substantial across the five continents. ## The five continents ### Avarra — principal campaign continent Avarra is the main setting of Gloin Hammerfeld's current campaign. Its major geographical and political features include: - The Ironspine Mountains and the Seven Khazari Mountain Thrones in the central mountain systems. - Letharion, the western Eldar forest realm. - Urakai territories, plains and highlands to the east. - The human kingdoms of Aldermere and Valtoria in the southwest and frontier regions. - Merchant Republics and southern trade routes. - Southern approaches toward Sahrad and the Southern Sultanates. - Northern territories and the Northern Holds. Avarra contains the current campaign locations Karak-Varn, the eastern mine, Crownward and the Silver Anvil workshop. Its full political borders, exact coordinates and detailed map remain open for development. ### Tharvorn A northern continent characterised by cold forests, tundra, snow-covered mountain ranges, frozen lakes and broad plains. Its distances, political divisions and principal settlements have not yet been fully mapped. ### Sahrad A southern continent of great deserts, fertile river valleys, tropical coasts, mountain plateaus, ancient cities and savannah. It includes the wider cultural sphere of the Southern Sultanates. Local environments and cultures vary considerably. ### Orundel An eastern continent of grasslands, highland plateaus, jungles, great rivers and ancient ruins. Its internal political map and many of its ancient sites remain unknown or undeveloped. ### Vaelora A western continent of forests, rugged coasts, great lakes, a mountainous interior, ancient woodland and territories that remain unexplored or poorly documented. ## Seas, oceans and major waters The following names are established geographical labels in the worldbuilding. Their exact positions, boundaries, coastlines and routes should be placed only when a reliable map is developed: - Western Ocean - Eastern Ocean - Southern Ocean - Northern Ocean - Crown Sea - Shattered Isles - Sapphire Strait - Stormward Sea - Deepwater Reaches Major rivers named in the setting include the Great Veyr, Silverflow, King's River and Sahradi River. Their complete courses, tributaries, exact source locations and mouths remain to be mapped. ## Mountain ranges, forests, plains and regions Established major geographical names include: - Ironspine Mountains — central Avarran mountain system and home of the Seven Khazari Mountain Thrones. - Worldbreak Range - Crownwall Mountains - Emberback Mountains - Letharion — western Eldar forest realm. - Elderwood - Green Expanse - Ashenwood - Eastern Grasslands - Golden Reach - Northern Steppe - Valtorian Marches - Sunscorched Expanse - Glass Desert - Red Wastes These names are established, but not all have fully defined borders, populations, routes or political ownership. Do not invent exact placements or distances simply to fill a map. ## The Seven Khazari Mountain Thrones The Khazari are a thriving dwarven civilisation of approximately 24 million people, with common lifespans of around 300–450 years. They are organised among seven powerful, culturally distinct and politically independent mountain thrones. They share deep traditions of mining, engineering, craftsmanship and runic work, but they are not one uniform kingdom. The other six thrones have not yet been fully detailed in the current reference. Their names, rulers, populations, alliances and precise locations must be developed individually rather than guessed. ### Karak-Varn Karak-Varn is one of the Seven Thrones and the current campaign's principal city. - Population: Approximately 22.8 million in the current sixfold demographic model (3.8 million was the superseded baseline). - Ruler: King Durgan IV Stonehand. - King's age: 214. - Reign: 86 years. - Setting: A vast Khazari mountain city and royal seat within the Ironspine region. Known districts and landmarks: - Crownward: Administrative and royal government quarter. - Ironmarket: Commercial district, including the Copper Kettle tavern. - Upper Artisan Quarter: Specialist workshops, including Maela Deepforge's Silver Anvil. - Lower Artisan District: Residential and craft district, including Edda Coppervein's home. - Great Stair: Major civic landmark. - Hall of Seven: Major civic landmark. - Royal Historical Archive: Repository of historical records and restricted research. - Iron Circle: Military training complex where Sergeant Keldrun Broadshield teaches civilians. - Old Quarry Access: Quarry site where Borin Ashmantle teaches Gloin practical engineering. The precise street plan, scale of districts, routes, gates and full layout remain to be documented. Do not pretend a schematic description is a surveyed city map. ## Ironspine and the eastern mine location Several leagues beneath the Ironspine lies an abandoned eastern mine, officially sealed 63 years ago after reported collapses. It is a significant current campaign location, but detailed physical evidence and the mine mystery are documented separately in the History & Ancient Lore and Campaign Chronicle pages. Known geographical facts: - The mine is in the Ironspine region. - Public maps show six levels. - Borin Ashmantle's older survey records nine levels. - The lower galleries include engineered passages and chambers predating the mine itself. - The Hall Beneath the Mountain lies beneath level nine and is connected by a narrow passage to a sealed First Throne doorway. Do not treat the lower levels as ordinary open mine workings. The mine is closed, restricted and under investigation. ## The Deepways — Khazari underground road network The Khazari maintain an ancient system of underground highways known collectively as the Deepways. They connect the Seven Mountain Thrones and link major mines, fortress-gates, subterranean settlements, engineering stations and trade depots. They are used by merchants, travellers, messengers, military forces and heavy freight. ### Construction and character - The Deepways are engineered routes, not simply natural cave passages. - They include immense excavated galleries, reinforced tunnels, vaulted halls, cut-throughs, bridges over chasms, gates, ventilation shafts, drainage works and waystations. - Some stretches are very old and predate the present Seven Thrones; others are later extensions, diversions or repairs built by individual kingdoms. - Main arteries can be broad enough for loaded freight wagons and organised military movement. - Secondary branches may be narrow, steep, old, partially collapsed or suitable only for foot traffic and pack animals. - The network is not uniformly safe or continuously maintained. Some routes are well-lit, guarded and busy; others are abandoned, disputed, damaged, sealed or hazardous. ### Trade and strategic importance - The Deepways are vital to Khazari trade and political connection. - They carry bulk goods such as ore, metal, stone, grain, timber and crafted products between mountain realms without relying entirely on exposed surface routes. - They provide strategic routes for messengers, reinforcements and supply columns. - Control of a major junction, gate or tunnel can carry enormous military and economic value. - Toll rights, maintenance obligations, customs inspections, access treaties and junction control are political matters. The Seven Thrones cooperate where useful but retain distinct laws and interests. - Merchants may prefer a longer maintained route over a shorter dangerous one. Freight rates, tolls, escorts, delays and closures affect prices in connected markets. ### Limits and dangers - The network is not one uninterrupted, perfectly mapped highway. Routes have dead ends, sealed branches, forgotten junctions and sections with incomplete records. - Natural hazards include rockfalls, flooding, gas pockets, underground fires, unstable supports and deep chasms. - Other dangers may include bandits, hostile creatures, abandoned machinery and political blockades. - Ancient sections may contain First Throne construction or systems whose purpose is not understood. This does not mean every Deepway tunnel is First Throne-built or connected to the eastern mine mystery. - Some passages are restricted to a throne's authorities, guilds or military. Others are open to licensed merchants and travellers. The full route map, exact total length, age of each branch, toll schedules, travel times and current conditions remain to be developed. Do not assume every throne has a direct, open route to every other throne; some journeys may require transfers, surface travel or passage through a third kingdom. ## Distance and travel scale These are broad worldbuilding scales for planning, not exact measured routes: | Scale | Approximate distance | | --- | --- | | Local or regional journey | 100–300 km | | Between neighbouring major cities | 300–800 km | | Between kingdoms | 800–2,000 km | | Across a large region | 2,000–3,500 km | | Across a continent | 4,000–7,000 km | | Around the planet | about 42,000 km | Typical daily travel ranges under reasonable conditions: | Travel mode | Approximate daily distance | | --- | --- | | Walking | 20–30 km | | Loaded wagon | 20–35 km | | Passenger coach | 40–65 km | | Riding horse | 40–70 km | | Relay horse | 80–120 km | | Sailing vessel | 100–200 km | | Deepways caravan | 40–80 km | | Gyrocopter | Varies by model, weather, load and purpose | Terrain, weather, road and tunnel condition, security, elevation, traffic, freight, rest and fatigue all affect travel. These ranges are not guarantees. Do not calculate an exact arrival time without considering the actual route and circumstances. ## Map and geographical canon boundaries - The geography is currently a structured schematic, not a fully surveyed atlas. - Do not invent exact coordinates, borders, coastlines, route lengths or city-to-city distances that have not been established. - Continent descriptions and regional names are canon; many internal details remain open. - A named landmark does not automatically establish its precise position relative to every other landmark. - When a map is eventually produced, it should be treated as a new canonical reference only after its geography is reconciled with this page. - New settlements, mountain systems, seas, rivers and roads should be added with their location, scale, local context and evidence status. ## Small villages, hamlets and hidden communities Beyond the great cities, kingdoms and major trade routes, Eryndor contains — and should continue to develop — a dispersed pattern of small settlements belonging to lesser magical peoples and other local communities. These may include villages, hamlets, family steadings, burrow-settlements, woodland enclaves, cave hamlets and modest coastal or underwater communities. Their potential distribution is broad: forests and woodland margins, plains and grassland edges, river valleys, hills, marshes, mountain foothills, natural caverns and underground networks, islands, reefs and suitable ocean environments across all five continents. Not every habitat will suit every people. Underwater settlements, for example, require inhabitants and construction adapted to submerged life; underground communities need viable water, air, food, access and protection. Most such places should be small in scale and locally distinctive. Some may be hidden or difficult to reach; others may trade with nearby towns, use seasonal markets, share paths or tunnels, or maintain old agreements with larger neighbours. A hamlet may consist of only a handful of households, while a village may support local crafts, food production, a meeting place or a small market. Their political organisation need not resemble that of a kingdom. This is an approved settlement-worldbuilding direction. It does not establish the exact additional species roster, settlement names, coordinates, populations or borders. Develop those individually and preserve the distinction between established peoples, approved additions, rumours and unplaced concepts. The geographical map remains schematic; do not assign precise locations without mapping them.
